title: Hypothesis Testing
description: Null and alternative hypotheses, chi-squared tests for independence and goodness of fit, one-sample and two-sample t-tests, paired t-tests, binomial and Poisson hypothesis testing, Type I & II errors, and Spearman's rank correlation.

notes.heading: The Language of Hypothesis Testing
notes.body:
A hypothesis test uses sample data to decide whether there is enough evidence to reject a claim about a population parameter or distribution.

📌 Definition
The null hypothesis $H_0$ is the statement of "no change" or "no effect" that you assume to be true at the start of the test.
The alternative hypothesis $H_1$ is what you suspect might be true instead.

🔑 Key Terms
    Significance level $\alpha$ — the probability threshold you choose before the test (commonly 1%, 5% or 10%).
    $p$-value — the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming $H_0$ is true.
    Critical region — the set of test-statistic values that would lead you to reject $H_0$.

💡 Worked Example
A researcher suspects that students at a school sleep fewer than the recommended 8 hours per night. A sample of 50 students yields a mean of 7.4 hours and a $p$-value of 0.018 for a one-tailed test.

  Step 1: Write the hypotheses
    $H_0: \mu = 8$ hours
    $H_1: \mu < 8$ hours

  Step 2: Compare the $p$-value with $\alpha$
    $\alpha = 0.05$
    $p = 0.018$
    Since $0.018 < 0.05$, we reject $H_0$.

  Step 3: Write the conclusion
    There is sufficient evidence to suggest that students sleep fewer than 8 hours per night on average.

📎 One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed Tests
• One-tailed test — used when you are specifically looking for an increase or a decrease.
• Two-tailed test — used when you are looking for any change, regardless of direction.

📎 How to Word Conclusions
• If $p < \alpha$: "There is sufficient evidence to suggest that..."
• If $p > \alpha$: "There is insufficient evidence to suggest that..."
• Never write "accept $H_1$" or "prove $H_0$ is true".

⚠️ Common Mistake
Choosing a one-tailed test after looking at the data. You must decide the direction before collecting the sample, otherwise you artificially inflate the chance of a significant result.

illustration.alt: Null and alternative hypotheses explained; the p-value compared to significance level α; Type I and Type II errors with a decision table; and critical regions for two-tailed tests.
illustration.caption: Hypothesis testing uses sample data to decide whether to reject H₀. The p-value is the probability of observing your result if H₀ is true. Reject H₀ if p ≤ α.

notes.heading: Chi-Squared Tests
notes.body:
The chi-squared ($\chi^2$) test compares observed frequencies with the frequencies you would expect if a certain model were true. It is used either to test for independence between two categorical variables or to check how well a distribution fits a set of data.

📌 Chi-Squared Test for Independence
This test determines whether two categorical variables are associated.
    Expected frequency:     $E = \dfrac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}$
    Degrees of freedom:     $\nu = (m-1)(n-1)$    for an $m \times n$ contingency table
    Test statistic:         $\chi^2_{\text{calc}} = \sum \dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$

💡 Worked Example — Independence
A survey of 100 students records favourite subject by gender.

            Math   Science   Total
  Male       30      20       50
  Female     25      25       50
  Total      55      45      100

Test at the 5% level whether subject preference is independent of gender.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0$: Subject preference is independent of gender.
    $H_1$: Subject preference is not independent of gender.

  Step 2: Calculate expected frequencies
    $E(\text{Male}, \text{Math}) = \dfrac{50 \times 55}{100} = 27.5$
    $E(\text{Male}, \text{Science}) = \dfrac{50 \times 45}{100} = 22.5$
    $E(\text{Female}, \text{Math}) = \dfrac{50 \times 55}{100} = 27.5$
    $E(\text{Female}, \text{Science}) = \dfrac{50 \times 45}{100} = 22.5$

  Step 3: Find degrees of freedom
    $\nu = (2-1)(2-1) = 1$

  Step 4: Compute $\chi^2$ and the $p$-value
    $\chi^2_{\text{calc}} \approx 1.01$
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.315$

  Step 5: Decide and conclude
    $0.315 > 0.05$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest that subject preference and gender are associated.

📌 Chi-Squared Goodness of Fit Test
This test checks whether sample data follows a claimed distribution (uniform, binomial, normal or Poisson).
    Degrees of freedom:     $\nu = k-1$    for $k$ categories
    If you estimate a parameter from the data, subtract 1 extra degree of freedom for each parameter estimated.

💡 Worked Example — Goodness of Fit (Uniform)
A salesman records weekly car sales over six weeks: 15, 17, 11, 21, 14, 12.
Test at the 5% level whether sales are uniformly distributed.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0$: Sales are uniformly distributed.
    $H_1$: Sales are not uniformly distributed.

  Step 2: Calculate expected frequencies
    Total sales = 90
    Expected for each week = $90 \div 6 = 15$

  Step 3: Find degrees of freedom
    $\nu = 6-1 = 5$

  Step 4: Compute $\chi^2$ and the $p$-value
    $$\chi^2_{\text{calc}} = \dfrac{(15-15)^2}{15} + \dfrac{(17-15)^2}{15} + \dfrac{(11-15)^2}{15} + \dfrac{(21-15)^2}{15} + \dfrac{(14-15)^2}{15} + \dfrac{(12-15)^2}{15}$$
            $\approx 4.40$
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.493$

  Step 5: Decide and conclude
    $0.493 > 0.05$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest that sales are not uniform.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Every expected frequency must be greater than 5. Combine rows or columns if necessary.
• For independence, enter observed data as a matrix on your GDC.
• For goodness of fit, enter observed and expected values as two separate lists.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to reduce degrees of freedom when you estimate parameters (e.g. estimating $p$ for a binomial or $\mu$ for a Poisson distribution from the sample).

notes.heading: t-Tests for Means
notes.body:
Use a $t$-test when the population variance is unknown and must be estimated from the sample. Your GDC can perform one-sample, two-sample and paired $t$-tests.

📌 One-Sample $t$-Test
Tests a population mean $\mu$ when $\sigma^2$ is unknown.
    Test statistic follows a $t$-distribution with $df = n-1$.
    $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$

📌 Two-Sample $t$-Test (Pooled)
Compares the means of two independent normal populations.
    You assume the unknown variances are equal.
    $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$

📌 Paired $t$-Test
Used when two measurements are taken from the same subject (e.g. before and after).
    Calculate the difference for each pair.
    Perform a one-sample $t$-test on the differences.
    $H_0: \mu_D = 0$

💡 Worked Example — One-Sample $t$-Test
The IQ of students at a school is normally distributed with mean 126. After playing classical music at lunch, a sample of 15 students has mean IQ 127.1 and sample variance 14.7. Test at 5% whether the mean has changed.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: \mu = 126$
    $H_1: \mu \neq 126$    (two-tailed)

  Step 2: Find the unbiased estimate of variance
    $\text{Unbiased estimate} = \dfrac{n}{n-1} \times \text{sample variance}$
    $\text{Unbiased estimate} = \dfrac{15}{14} \times 14.7 = 15.75$

  Step 3: Enter data into GDC
    One-sample $t$-test with $\bar{x} = 127.1$, $s = \sqrt{15.75}$, $n = 15$
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.301$

  Step 4: Decide and conclude
    $0.301 > 0.05$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest that the mean IQ has changed.

💡 Worked Example — Paired $t$-Test
Nine students take tests in French and Spanish. The scores are:

  Student   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8   9
  French   61  82  77  80  99  69  75  71  81
  Spanish  74  79  83  66  95  79  82  81  85

Test at the 10% level whether there is a difference in mean scores.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: \mu_D = 0$    (no difference)
    $H_1: \mu_D \neq 0$    (two-tailed)

  Step 2: Calculate differences (French $-$ Spanish)
    $-13$, 3, $-6$, 14, 4, $-10$, $-7$, $-10$, $-4$

  Step 3: Enter differences into GDC as a single list
    One-sample $t$-test on the differences
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.27$

  Step 4: Decide and conclude
    $0.27 > 0.10$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest a difference in mean scores between the two subjects.

💡 Worked Example — Two-Sample $t$-Test
Puzzle completion times (minutes) are recorded for children and adults.

  Children: 3.1, 2.7, 3.5, 3.1, 2.9, 3.2, 3.0, 2.9
  Adults:   3.1, 3.6, 3.5, 3.6, 2.9, 3.6, 3.4, 3.6, 3.7, 3.0

Test at the 1% level whether children are generally faster.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$
    $H_1: \mu_1 < \mu_2$    (one-tailed)

  Step 2: Choose the test
    Population variances unknown $\rightarrow$ pooled two-sample $t$-test

  Step 3: Enter data into GDC
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.004$

  Step 4: Decide and conclude
    $0.004 < 0.01$, so we reject $H_0$.
    There is sufficient evidence to suggest that children complete the puzzle faster than adults.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always check whether the data is paired before choosing a test.
• For paired data, use the differences — do not ignore the pairing.
• A two-sample test assumes the two groups are independent.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using a two-sample $t$-test on paired data. This ignores the natural pairing and makes the test less powerful, so you may miss a real effect.

notes.heading: Binomial, Poisson and Type I & II Errors
notes.body:
Some hypothesis tests use discrete distributions, and every test carries a risk of reaching the wrong conclusion. Spearman's rank correlation offers a robust way to measure monotonic relationships.

📌 Binomial Hypothesis Test
Used to test whether the proportion of a population with a certain characteristic has increased or decreased.
    $H_0: p = p_0$
    $H_1: p < p_0$  or  $p > p_0$    (one-tailed only in IB DP)
    Test statistic: $x =$ number of successes in $n$ trials
    $p$-value $= P(X \leq x)$ for $H_1: p < p_0$
    $p$-value $= P(X \geq x)$ for $H_1: p > p_0$     where $X \sim B(n, p_0)$

💡 Worked Example — Binomial
A coin is suspected of bias towards heads. In 20 tosses there are 14 heads. Test at the 5% level whether $p > 0.5$.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: p = 0.5$
    $H_1: p > 0.5$

  Step 2: Identify the test statistic
    $x = 14$

  Step 3: Calculate the $p$-value
    $p$-value $= P(X \geq 14)$ where $X \sim B(20, 0.5)$
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.0577$

  Step 4: Decide and conclude
    $0.0577 > 0.05$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest the coin is biased towards heads.

📌 Poisson Hypothesis Test
Used to test whether the mean number of occurrences in a fixed period has changed.
    $H_0: m = m_0$
    $H_1: m < m_0$  or  $m > m_0$    (one-tailed only in IB DP)
    Test statistic: $x =$ observed count
    $p$-value $= P(X \leq x)$ for $H_1: m < m_0$
    $p$-value $= P(X \geq x)$ for $H_1: m > m_0$     where $X \sim \text{Po}(m_0)$

💡 Worked Example — Poisson
A call centre usually receives 4 calls per hour. One hour only 2 calls are received. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has decreased.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: m = 4$
    $H_1: m < 4$

  Step 2: Identify the test statistic
    $x = 2$

  Step 3: Calculate the $p$-value
    $p$-value $= P(X \leq 2)$ where $X \sim \text{Po}(4)$
    $p\text{-value} \approx 0.238$

  Step 4: Decide and conclude
    $0.238 > 0.05$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest the mean number of calls has decreased.

📌 Type I and Type II Errors
    Type I error — rejecting $H_0$ when it is actually true (false positive).
    Type II error — failing to reject $H_0$ when it is actually false (false negative).
    For continuous distributions:     $P(\text{Type I}) = \alpha$
    For discrete distributions:       $P(\text{Type I}) \leq \alpha$
Lowering $\alpha$ reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error.

📌 Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient ($r_s$)
Measures the strength of a monotonic relationship between two variables using ranked data.
    $r_s$ is simply the PMCC calculated on the ranks.
    $r_s = 1$ means the data is strictly increasing.
    $r_s = -1$ means the data is strictly decreasing.
    It is robust to outliers and can be used when the original data is not linear.

💡 Worked Example — Spearman's Rank
Two judges rank five artworks:

  Artwork   A   B   C   D   E
  Judge 1   1   2   3   4   5
  Judge 2   2   1   4   3   5

  Step 1: Enter the ranks as two lists in your GDC
  Step 2: Calculate the PMCC of the ranks
    $r_s \approx 0.80$
  Step 3: Interpret
    There is a strong positive monotonic correlation between the two judges' rankings.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Binomial and Poisson hypothesis tests in the IB are one-tailed only.
• For discrete distributions, the probability of a Type I error is at most $\alpha$, not necessarily equal to it.
• Use Spearman's when the relationship may be monotonic but not linear, or when data is given as ranks.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using Pearson's PMCC on ranked or clearly non-linear data. Pearson's only measures linear correlation and is sensitive to outliers, whereas Spearman's measures monotonic trends.

notes.heading: The Critical-Value Approach
notes.body:
Besides comparing a $p$-value with $\alpha$, you can also decide a hypothesis test by comparing the test statistic with a critical value. The two methods always lead to the same conclusion.

📌 Definition
The critical-value approach rejects $H_0$ whenever the test statistic falls in the critical region, i.e. beyond a critical value chosen so that the critical region has total area $\alpha$.

🔑 How it works
    Find the critical value(s) from the appropriate distribution using the significance level $\alpha$.
    For a one-tailed test, put all of $\alpha$ in one tail.
    For a two-tailed test, split $\alpha$ equally between both tails ($\alpha/2$ in each).
    If the test statistic lies beyond the critical value, reject $H_0$.

💡 Worked Example
A two-tailed $z$-test is carried out at the 5% level and the test statistic is $z = -2.34$.

  Step 1: Find the critical values
    $\alpha/2 = 0.025$ in each tail.
    Critical values are $\pm z_{0.025} \approx \pm 1.96$.

  Step 2: Compare the test statistic
    $-2.34 < -1.96$, so the statistic lies in the critical region.

  Step 3: Conclude
    Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence to suggest the mean has changed.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The critical-value approach and the $p$-value approach are equivalent: rejecting with one means rejecting with the other.
• Use inverse-normal, inverse-$t$ or $\chi^2$ tables on your GDC to find critical values.
• Always state the critical region when using this method.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Comparing a test statistic with $\alpha$ or a $p$-value with a critical value. Compare like with like: test statistic vs critical value, or $p$-value vs $\alpha$.

notes.heading: $z$-Tests for Means and Proportions
notes.body:
A $z$-test is used when the test statistic can be modelled by a normal distribution. This happens when the population variance is known, or when the sample is large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to apply.

📌 One-Sample $z$-Test for a Mean
Use when the population is normal (or $n$ is large) and $\sigma^2$ is known.
    $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$
    Test statistic:     $z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$

📌 One-Sample $z$-Test for a Proportion
Use when testing a population proportion with a sufficiently large sample.
    $H_0: p = p_0$
    Test statistic:     $z = \dfrac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$

💡 Worked Example — Proportion
A company claims that 30% of customers prefer its new flavour. In a random sample of 200 customers, 72 prefer it. Test at the 5% level whether the proportion differs from 30%.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: p = 0.30$
    $H_1: p \neq 0.30$

  Step 2: Calculate the test statistic
    $\hat{p} = 72/200 = 0.36$
    $$z = \dfrac{0.36 - 0.30}{\sqrt{0.30 \times 0.70 / 200}} \approx 1.85$$

  Step 3: Find the $p$-value
    Two-tailed $p$-value $\approx 0.064$

  Step 4: Decide and conclude
    $0.064 > 0.05$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.
    There is insufficient evidence to suggest the proportion differs from 30%.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Use a $z$-test when $\sigma^2$ is known or when $n$ is large.
• For proportions, check that $np_0$ and $n(1-p_0)$ are both greater than 5.
• A two-tailed test looks for any difference; a one-tailed test looks for increase or decrease.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using a $t$-test when the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is actually known. With known $\sigma$, the test statistic follows a normal distribution, not a $t$-distribution.

notes.heading: Spearman's Rank Correlation Hypothesis Test
notes.body:
Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$ measures the strength of a monotonic relationship between two variables. You can test whether the population rank correlation $\rho_s$ is different from zero.

📌 Definition
$r_s$ is Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient calculated on the ranks of the data rather than the raw values. It takes values from $-1$ to $1$.

🔑 How it works
    Rank each variable separately, averaging tied ranks.
    Calculate the PMCC of the ranks to obtain $r_s$.
    State $H_0: \rho_s = 0$ and a one- or two-tailed alternative.
    Compare $|r_s|$ with the critical value from tables or use the $p$-value from your GDC.

💡 Worked Example
Ten students are ranked by height and by exam score. The calculated value is $r_s = 0.71$. Test at the 5% level whether there is a positive monotonic correlation.

  Step 1: State the hypotheses
    $H_0: \rho_s = 0$
    $H_1: \rho_s > 0$

  Step 2: Identify the test statistic
    $r_s = 0.71$

  Step 3: Compare with the critical value
    For $n = 10$ at 5% one-tailed, the critical value is approximately $0.564$.
    Since $0.71 > 0.564$, reject $H_0$.

  Step 4: Conclude
    There is sufficient evidence of a positive monotonic relationship between height and exam score.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Use Spearman's when the relationship may be monotonic but not linear, or when data is given as ranks.
• It is robust to outliers because it uses ranks rather than raw values.
• Always average tied ranks before calculating $r_s$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying Pearson's PMCC to ranked or clearly non-linear data. Pearson's only measures linear correlation, whereas Spearman's measures monotonic trends.

flashcards.example: $p = 0.03$ means a 3% chance of seeing this result if $H_0$ were true.

flashcards.definition: $\chi^2_{\text{calc}} = \sum \dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$. It measures how far observed frequencies differ from expected frequencies.
flashcards.example: A large $\chi^2$ value suggests the variables are not independent.

flashcards.definition: For independence: $\nu = (\text{rows}-1)(\text{cols}-1)$. For goodness of fit: $\nu = k-1$ (minus 1 more per estimated parameter).
Tests a population mean when $\sigma^2$ is unknown, using the $t$-distribution with $df = n-1$.
flashcards.example: Testing whether the mean height of a class differs from 170 cm.

flashcards.definition: Tests the mean difference between two paired sets of data by treating the differences as a single sample.
flashcards.example: Comparing students' scores before and after a revision course.

flashcards.term: Type I and Type II errors
flashcards.definition: Type I: rejecting a true $H_0$ (false positive). Type II: failing to reject a false $H_0$ (false negative).
flashcards.example: A medical test saying you are sick when you are healthy is a Type I error.

flashcards.definition: A value from the sampling distribution that marks the boundary of the critical region for a given significance level $\alpha$.
flashcards.example: For a two-tailed $z$-test at 5%, the critical values are $\pm 1.96$.

flashcards.definition: The set of values of the test statistic that would lead you to reject the null hypothesis $H_0$.
flashcards.example: $|z| > 1.96$ is the critical region for a two-tailed $z$-test at 5%.

flashcards.definition: A test of $H_0: p = p_0$ using the statistic $z = \dfrac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$, valid for large samples.
flashcards.example: Testing whether more than 60% of voters support a policy based on a sample of 500 voters.

flashcards.definition: The PMCC calculated on ranked data; it measures the strength of a monotonic relationship and is robust to outliers.
flashcards.example: $r_s = 0.85$ indicates a strong positive monotonic association between two ranked variables.

questions.stem: In a hypothesis test, the $p$-value is found to be 0.032. The test is carried out at the 5% significance level. What is the correct conclusion?
questions.explanation: When the $p$-value is less than the significance level ($0.032 < 0.05$), we reject the null hypothesis $H_0$. We never "accept" $H_1$ definitively — we only say there is sufficient evidence against $H_0$.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a Type I error?
choices: Failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is false
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a "false positive" — rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true. A Type II error is failing to reject $H_0$ when it is false.

questions.stem: A contingency table for favourite sport vs gender has 3 rows (sports) and 2 columns (gender). What is the number of degrees of freedom for a $\chi^2$ test for independence?
questions.explanation: For a chi-squared test for independence, $\nu = (m-1)(n-1) = (3-1)(2-1) = 2 \times 1 = 2$.

questions.stem: A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test is conducted with 5 categories to test whether data follows a uniform distribution. What are the degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: For a goodness of fit test with $k$ categories, $\nu = k-1 = 5-1 = 4$. No parameters need estimating for a uniform distribution.

questions.stem: A researcher records the blood pressure of 8 patients before and after taking a new medication. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Since each patient is measured twice (before and after), the data is paired. Calculate the differences and use a paired $t$-test. A two-sample test would ignore the pairing and be less powerful.

questions.stem: In a binomial hypothesis test, $H_0: p = 0.4$ and $H_1: p > 0.4$. In 20 trials there are 12 successes. What is the $p$-value?
questions.explanation: For $H_1: p > 0.4$, "at least as extreme" means 12 or more successes. The $p$-value is $P(X \geq 12)$ where $X \sim B(20, 0.4)$.

questions.stem: The expected frequency for a cell in a contingency table is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Expected frequency $E = \dfrac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}$. This assumes the two variables are independent.

questions.stem: Which statement about Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is true?
choices: It requires the original data to be normally distributed
It is robust to outliers and can detect monotonic relationships
It always gives the same value as Pearson's PMCC
questions.explanation: Spearman's uses ranked data, so it measures monotonic (consistently increasing or decreasing) relationships and is not greatly affected by outliers. Pearson's only measures linear correlation and is sensitive to outliers.

questions.stem: A one-sample $t$-test is used instead of a $z$-test when:
choices: The population is not normally distributed
questions.explanation: A $t$-test is used when the population variance $\sigma^2$ is unknown and must be estimated from the sample. If $\sigma^2$ is known, use a $z$-test. For large $n$, the $t$-distribution approximates the normal distribution.

questions.stem: In a two-sample $t$-test comparing the means of two independent groups, the null hypothesis is:
questions.explanation: $H_0$ always states "no effect" or "no difference": $\mu_1 = \mu_2$. $H_1$ would be $\mu_1 < \mu_2$, $\mu_1 > \mu_2$, or $\mu_1 \neq \mu_2$ depending on the context.

questions.stem: In a two-tailed $z$-test at the 5% significance level, the test statistic is $z = 2.10$. What is the correct conclusion using the critical-value approach?
questions.explanation: For a two-tailed test at 5%, the critical values are $\pm 1.96$. Since $2.10 > 1.96$, the test statistic lies in the critical region, so we reject $H_0$.

questions.stem: A researcher knows the population standard deviation $\sigma$ and has a large random sample. Which test is most appropriate for the population mean?
questions.explanation: When $\sigma$ is known and the sample is large (or the population is normal), use a one-sample $z$-test for the mean. A $t$-test is used when $\sigma$ is unknown.

questions.stem: A politician claims that 45% of voters support a new policy. In a random sample of 300 voters, 150 support it. What is the value of $\hat{p}$ used in the $z$-test?
questions.explanation: The sample proportion is $\hat{p} = 150/300 = 0.50$. The value $0.45$ is the hypothesised proportion $p_0$ under $H_0$.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of Spearman's rank correlation coefficient?
choices: To test whether two variables are linearly related using raw data
To measure the strength of a monotonic relationship using ranked data
To compare the means of two independent samples
To test whether a sample follows a uniform distribution
questions.explanation: Spearman's $r_s$ is the PMCC of the ranks, so it measures monotonic relationships and is robust to outliers. Pearson's $r$ measures linear relationships using raw data.

questions.stem: If the significance level $\alpha$ is decreased from 5% to 1%, what happens to the probability of a Type II error, all else being equal?
questions.explanation: Decreasing $\alpha$ makes it harder to reject $H_0$, which reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error.
